extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and design patent applicants/agents
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards for examination and prosecution of U.S. design patent applications, including drawing/specification requirements, 35 U.S.C. §112 enablement/definiteness rules, new-matter limits, and restriction practice under 35 U.S.C. §121.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of visual disclosure (drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the visual disclosure of the claimed design as originally filed is of such poor quality that its overall shape and appearance cannot be understood, applicant should be advised that the claim might be fatally defective (use form paragraph 15.65).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise applicant and consider form paragraph 15.65; poor drawings may make the claim fatally defective because overall shape/appearance cannot be determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of narrative description to supplement drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative description in the specification can supplement the drawing disclosure to define the scope of protection sought; such description is incorporated into the claim by the use of language 'and described' therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the description refers to embodiments or modified forms not shown in the drawing, or uses vague/nondescriptive words like 'variations' and 'equivalents', or states the claimed design is not limited to the exact shape and appearance shown, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, as nonenabling and indefinite. Form paragraph 15.21 may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undisclosed visible surfaces/portions not part of claimed design
rubrics_metrics.description: Any part of the article not shown in the drawing or described in the specification forms no part of the claimed design (In re Zahn). Determination of patentability is based on the design shown and described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portions are not shown/described, they are excluded from the claimed design; use appropriate form language to indicate which surfaces/portions are not shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 (first and second paragraphs) — general
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, when the claimed invention is not described in full, clear, concise and exact terms to enable one skilled in the art to make and use it and when it fails to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 15.21 and provide a complete explanation of the basis for the rejection in the Office action (bracket 1). Do not use this form paragraph when separate specific rejections under the first and/or second paragraph are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestions to overcome 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may submit large, clear informal drawings or photographs showing the unclear areas, or disclaim indefinite areas by converting them to broken lines and amending the specification to state those portions form no part of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to 35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121; identify unclear areas in bracketed instruction. Alternative is to disclaim portions via broken lines and include a statement in the specification that those portions form no part of claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment may not be possible (fatal defect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim might be fatally defective; that is, it might not be possible to [correct/clarify] without introducing new matter (35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 15.65 to indicate portions insufficiently disclosed and that correction would introduce new matter; identify the insufficiently disclosed portion in the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter prohibition and antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: New matter is subject matter which has no antecedent basis in the original specification, drawings or claim. An amendment to the claim must have antecedent basis in the original disclosure; otherwise it introduces new matter and must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A change in configuration (including removal of three-dimensional surface treatment integral to configuration) introduces prohibited new matter (In re Salmon). Conversion of broken to solid lines or reduction to broken lines may be permissible only if the underlying configuration was fully disclosed and enabling in the original filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible and impermissible amendments (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible amendments include preliminary amendments specifically identified in the original oath/declaration and disclaimers included in the original filing; impermissible amendments include claim changes without antecedent basis that change configuration or surface appearance by adding previously undisclosed matter (In re Berkman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the amendment departs from the original disclosure; permissible examples and impermissible examples are given in the MPEP. If impermissible, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must specifically identify asserted new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When an amendment is made that introduces new matter, the examiner should specifically identify in the Office action the subject matter not supported by the original disclosure; a mere generalization is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify differences/changes that introduce new matter and, if possible, suggest how to correct the amendment to overcome the rejection. Form paragraph 15.51 may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — indefiniteness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Defects in claim language give rise to a second paragraph rejection. Definiteness of claim language must be analyzed in light of prior art teachings and the application disclosure as interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art (In re Moore).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms of degree or broad language are not per se indefinite; evaluate each claim in context of the disclosure and prior art (see MPEP § 2173.05(b)). Use appropriate form paragraphs when scope cannot be determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of broadening phrases (e.g., 'or the like')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of phrases in the claim such as 'or similar article,' 'or the like,' or equivalent terminology has been held indefinite (Ex parte Pappas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a phrase appears in the claim/title and renders the claim indefinite, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112 second paragraph (form paragraph 15.22.02). However, similar language in the title directed to the environment of the article may not be the basis for rejection; see MPEP § 1503.01 subsection I. Examiner's amendment can remove such phrases (form paragraph 15.69.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection when scope cannot be determined from drawings/specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, should be made when the scope of protection sought by the claim cannot be determined from the designation of the design as shown in the drawing, referenced in the title and described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include unclear boundaries between claimed (solid lines) and unclaimed (broken lines) portions. Use form paragraph 15.22 and provide full explanation (bracket 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title must specify a known article of manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: The title must identify an article of manufacture; if the title fails to identify a known article and the drawing does not inherently identify it, the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph (Ex parte Strijland).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to clarify the title may introduce new matter (35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121). Use form paragraph 15.22.03 when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information required when title is ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: When the title of the article in which the design is embodied is too ambiguous, applicant is required to provide a sufficient explanation of the nature and intended use of the article so a proper classification and reliable search can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit information as a separate paper (not in the specification) and include analogous fields of search, pertinent prior art, advertising brochures, copending utility application numbers, etc. See 37 CFR 1.154(b)(1), 1.56, 1.97–1.99.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction practice under 35 U.S.C. 121 (single claim rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent application may only have a single claim. More than one embodiment may be protected by a single claim only if they involve a single inventive concept; otherwise restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 when multiple patentably distinct designs are claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner will require restriction whenever an application contains more than one patentably distinct design. The search/burden issue applicable to utility restrictions (MPEP § 803) is not applicable when determining restriction for design applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part test for patentable indistinctness of multiple embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple designs are not distinct inventions if: (A) the embodiments have overall appearances with basically the same design characteristics; and (B) the differences between the embodiments are insufficient to patentably distinguish one design from the other (differences may be de minimis or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both criteria are met, embodiments may be retained in a single application as obvious variations; if not met, restriction is required. Examiner may need to perform a prior art search to determine patentable distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent inventions — disparate articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Design inventions are independent if there is no apparent relationship between two or more disparate articles disclosed (e.g., eyeglasses and a door handle); restriction in such cases is clearly proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that design applications rarely disclose independent articles, but when present, restriction is appropriate (see MPEP § 806.06 for examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple embodiments — disclosure and antecedent basis requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple embodiments are disclosed, the specification should make clear that multiple embodiments are disclosed and particularize the differences between them. If one embodiment relies on another for completeness, differences must be identified in figure descriptions or by a descriptive statement in the specification as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent such statements, disclosure of one embodiment will normally not provide antecedent basis for amendments to other embodiments. Provide clear figure descriptions (example language given) to incorporate disclosure of one embodiment into another when intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of obviousness-type double patenting standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) must be applied to determine whether multiple embodiments may be retained in a single application: first determine whether overall appearances are basically the same, then whether differences are minor or obvious in view of analogous prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If embodiments meet both considerations they may be retained; if not, restriction is required. If appearances are not basically the same, restriction must be required regardless of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction grouping and election requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When embodiments divide into patentably distinct groups of designs, restriction is required to one group under 35 U.S.C. 121. A reply must include an election of a single group for prosecution on the merits (37 CFR 1.143); failure to elect is nonresponsive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should identify groups and explain differences. If applicant traverses the requirement, present evidence showing groups are obvious variations; if groups are found not distinct but retained, any rejection of one group will apply equally to all embodiments. Use form paragraphs 15.27, 15.27.01, 15.27.02, 15.27.03 as appropriate.
